reasoning_traces.think:
Product measures arise from extending individual measures μ and ν onto the Cartesian product space X × Y, forming λ = μ × ν. This construction ensures that measurable rectangles A × B have finite measure whenever μ(A) < ∞ and ν(B) < ∞. The proof relies on monotone convergence for measure extension and σ-finiteness to cover arbitrary measurable sets with countable unions of finite rectangles. When σ-finiteness fails, as shown in example (1), the diagonal D = {(x,y): x=y} can yield unequal iterated integrals: ∫ μ(D_y) dν(y) = 0 vs ∫ ν(D_x) dμ(x) = 1, violating Fubini’s theorem. Example (2) demonstrates that even if both (X,S,μ) and (Y,T,ν) are complete and σ-finite, their product (X×Y, S×T, μ×ν) may fail to be complete—e.g., by considering a non-measurable subset M ⊂ X and forming M × {y}. These insights reveal structural limitations in probabilistic modeling when foundational properties like σ-finiteness or completeness are absent.
